metadata.methods_description: Participants watched naturalistic emotion-eliciting multimedia videos while EEG, ECG and EMG were recorded. After each stimulus they gave feedback on self-assessment scales (valence, arousal, dominance, liking, familiarity, relevance, emotion category) with mouse clicks. Raw EEG is stored in EEGLAB .set/.fdt format with task events in TSV files. Python code was used for data collection and validation, and MATLAB for pre-processing.

citation_details.title: Dynamic Functional Connectivity of Emotion Processing in Beta Band with Naturalistic Emotion Stimuli
citation_details.author: Sudhakar Mishra, Narayanan Srinivasan, Uma Shanker Tiwary
citation_details.abstract: While naturalistic stimuli, such as movies, better represent the complexity of the real world and are perhaps crucial to understanding the dynamics of emotion processing, there is limited research on emotions with naturalistic stimuli. There is a need to understand the temporal dynamics of emotion processing and their relationship to different dimensions of emotion experience. In addition, there is a need to understand the dynamics of functional connectivity underlying different emotional experiences that occur during or prior to such experiences. To address these questions, we recorded the EEG of participants and asked them to mark the temporal location of their emotional experience as they watched a video. We also obtained self-assessment ratings for emotional multimedia stimuli. We calculated dynamic functional the connectivity (DFC) patterns in all the frequency bands, including information about hubs in the network. The change in functional networks was quantified in terms of temporal variability, which was then used in regression analysis to evaluate whether temporal variability in DFC (tvDFC) could predict different dimensions of emotional experience. We observed that the connectivity patterns in the upper beta band could differentiate emotion categories better during or prior to the reported emotional experience. The temporal variability in functional connectivity dynamics is primarily related to emotional arousal followed by dominance. The hubs in the functional networks were found across the right frontal and bilateral parietal lobes, which have been reported to facilitate affect, interoception, action, and memory-related processing. Since our study was performed with naturalistic real-life resembling emotional videos, the study contributes significantly to understanding the dynamics of emotion processing. The results support constructivist theories of emotional experience and show that changes in dynamic functional connectivity can predict aspects of our emotional experience.

citation_details.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Emotional Regulation in Patients with Various Disorders
citation_details.author: Mehta, Vedant
citation_details.abstract: Neurological and Physiological Disorders that impact emotional regulation each have their own unique characteristics which are important to understand in order to create a generalized solution to all of them. The purpose of this experiment is to explore the potential applications of EEG-based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) in enhancing emotional regulation for individuals with neurological and physiological disorders. The research focuses on the development of a novel neural network algorithm for understanding EEG data, with a particular emphasis on recognizing and regulating emotional states. The procedure involves the collection of EEG-based emotion data from open-Neuro. Using novel data modification techniques, information from the dataset can be altered to create a dataset that has neural patterns of patients with disorders whilst showing emotional change. The data analysis reveals promising results, as the algorithm is able to successfully classify emotional states with a high degree of accuracy. This suggests that EEG-based BCIs have the potential to be a valuable tool in aiding individuals with a range of neurological and physiological disorders in recognizing and regulating their emotions. To improve upon this work, data collection on patients with neurological disorders should be done to improve overall sample diversity.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

citation_details.title: Consciousness as OS and Applications: From Neural Primitive (Density × MA) to Higher-Order Emotions, Identity Formation, and Collective Cohesion
citation_details.author: 仁定 五十嵐
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Description This deposit provides the complete computational materials for Supplement S2 of the paper “Consciousness as OS and Applications” (v2.0, April 23, 2026). Contents • Core engine: DensityMA_OS_HigherOrderEmotions_Full_Integration_Final.py • 17 standalone Python simulation scripts (simulation_01_EmoEEG_MC.py 〜 simulation_17_extreme_physiological_states.py) • Generated high-resolution result graphs (PNG, 300 dpi) for each condition • Full Supplement S2 PDF and main paper PDF The simulations test the robustness of the zero-distance self-embrace loop (nostalgia repair, intentional divergence at the Edge of Chaos, identity shake detection, and Relation_MA dynamics) on top of the Density × MA OS layer. Seventeen diverse synthetic conditions are included, inspired by real neuroimaging datasets (ds005540 EmoEEG-MC, ds003751 DENS, ds007537 smartphone, psilocybin ds006072, TMS-EEG, joint musical hyperscanning, NDE-like surge, end-of-life decline, birth/sexual intimacy/acute illness, etc.). All simulations respect the brain’s ~20 W energy constraint through continuous gradient switching among GNWT, FEP, and IIT applications. Results consistently show Relation_MA stably remains in the ideal range 2.0–2.8 across all conditions, providing direct computational evidence for the paper’s central claim: humans cannot discard the self without ceasing to exist.
